01 / BACKGROUND

Does urban tree composition matter?

Urban tree species can differ substantially in canopy structure, phenology, and growth. These differences can influence ecosystem processes such as carbon storage and rainfall interception, susceptibility to drought, pests, and pathogens, and environmental exposures through allergenic pollen production and heat reduction from shade. Identifying the species composition of urban forests is therefore essential for evaluating their ecological and public-health implications.

Field surveys are the gold standard for urban tree mapping. However, the resulting inventories often have limitations in coverage, taxonomic resolution, positional accuracy, and acquisition date. Machine-learning models have the potential to classify millions of trees across cities using satellite observations, aerial imagery, canopy-height measurements, and weather data. However, many tree taxa share similar remotely observable characteristics, including height, canopy cover, and leaf-on period. Publicly available remote-sensing observations may therefore be better suited to classifying trees into distinguishable groups than identifying individual taxa.

This study developed and evaluated a two-stage modeling framework for classifying individual urban trees across U.S. cities using publicly available remote-sensing and meteorological data. The framework first identified taxon groups with distinguishable remote-sensing signatures, then trained a classifier to predict those fixed groups and evaluated its performance on held-out tree records.

02 / BUILDING A VIEW OF EACH TREE

Multiple datasets to identify and classify urban trees

Combining complementary data sources can improve the classification of urban trees. This study integrated municipal tree inventories with aerial imagery, elevation measurements, satellite observations, and weather-model estimates.

Example imagery of a northern red oak in Denver, Colorado.

03 / TREE CROWN MATCHING

Spatial alignment is important

Tree inventory coordinates often contain positional errors, sometimes exceeding 10 feet (approximately 3 m). For high-resolution datasets such as aerial imagery and LiDAR, accurately locating the tree crown center is essential for aligning observations of the same tree across datasets.

We used a tree detection algorithm to identify crown centers in aerial imagery and matched them to inventory coordinates within 5 m. We then extracted the inputs around these crown centers to align the datasets.

04 / LEARNING THE GROUPS

Which taxa are similar, and which are different?

Tree taxa can share canopy structure and seasonal patterns that limit their separation in remotely sensed data. We trained a model to identify groups of taxa with distinguishable combinations of observed characteristics using aerial imagery, canopy height, satellite observations, and weather data.

→→→
The embedding-space model was trained to identify features of the input data that distinguish tree taxa from one another. It combined 64 learned features into a 64-dimensional vector for each tree record, called an embedding.

05 / MAKING A PREDICTION

Predicting tree groups from multimodal observations

Once taxon groups were fixed, a second model was trained to classify individual trees from their aerial imagery, canopy height, satellite observations, and weather data. Probabilities for the 11 taxon groups were combined into six final reported groups.

→→→
For each tree, the model received aerial imagery, canopy-height data, satellite observations, and daily weather variables aligned to the crown center and observation dates.
TRAINING

Fit the classifier

1,590,460 records were used to learn the relationship between model inputs and the group labels.

VALIDATION

Select model checkpoints

At the end of each epoch, 100,000 records were used to evaluate model performance and save the top 5 epochs for ensemble model predictions.

TESTING

Evaluate predictions

A hold-out test dataset of 161,508 records were reserved for evaluating the final model performance.

07 / CONCLUSIONS

Multimodal observations can distinguish urban tree groups, but transfer across cities remains a challenge.

Combining aerial imagery, canopy height, satellite observations, and weather data supported the classification of individual urban trees into groups with similar embedding features. The results demonstrate the potential of publicly available data for characterizing urban tree composition, while identifying limits to taxonomic detail and geographic transfer.

TAXONOMIC RESOLUTION

Group taxa by observable similarities

The embedding-space model organized 579 taxa into 11 intermediate groups, including assignments for rare taxa. Combining intermediate-group probabilities produced six reported groups, providing a classification at the level supported by the observed features.

CLASSIFICATION PERFORMANCE

Most test records were classified correctly

The final model achieved 79.3% accuracy on 161,508 held-out records from represented cities. Confusion was greatest between Groups 2 and 3, indicating that some groups retained overlapping characteristics.

GEOGRAPHIC TRANSFER

Training across cities improved transfer

Accuracy declined when the target city was excluded from training and declined further for models trained in one source city. These results support using geographically diverse training data and evaluating performance locally before applying the model in a new city.

Taxon-group predictions could complement municipal inventories where field coverage is incomplete. Evaluating ecological processes or public-health exposures would additionally require information on the traits and species composition within each group, together with local validation of the predictions.

Study scope and interpretation

The analytical dataset contained 1,851,968 tree records representing 579 taxa across 36 U.S. cities. Group definitions were established before final model evaluation. The reported 79.3% accuracy describes the full held-out test dataset; group F1 scores and the misclassification matrix describe the 153,529-record height-screened subset.

The geographic box plots compare the same 22 eligible target cities under default, leave-one-city-out, and one-city-trained regimes. Their summary values are medians of city-level accuracy, rather than pooled record-level accuracy.

The groups describe similarity in the learned representations of the study inputs. They are not botanical ranks or validated ecological functional types. The interactive figures present study results and do not generate predictions for newly uploaded trees.
